title: Garbled readings
story: Bit rolls down the ramp into the basement and the water is ankle deep. The flood got into the terminals: they still answer, but some readings come out as nonsense. Door A wants the sum of the real numbers, and one crash on a bad reading means starting over.
power: Real data is messy. Someone types "x7" where a number was expected, a value is zero, a key is missing. Exceptions let your program notice the problem and choose what to do, instead of crashing. ### What an exception looks like When Python cannot do something, it raises an exception: it stops the program and prints an error report called a traceback. The last line names the exception type and explains the problem. ~~~text Traceback (most recent call last): File "main.py", line 1, in n = int("x7") ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'x7' ~~~ Common types: - ValueError: the right type but a bad value, like int("x7"). - ZeroDivisionError: dividing by zero. - KeyError: a dict key that does not exist. - TypeError: the wrong type, like "a" + 1. ### try and except Put risky code in a try: block. If an exception happens there, Python skips the rest of the block and jumps to the matching except block instead of crashing. If nothing goes wrong, the except block is skipped. ~~~python for text in ["12", "x7", "9"]: try: n = int(text) print("Got the number", n) except ValueError: print("Not a number:", text) print("Program still running") ~~~ - Line 3: int("12") works. For "x7", int() raises a ValueError right here. - Line 4: runs only if line 3 worked, so it is skipped for "x7". - Lines 5 to 6: run only when a ValueError happened in the try block. - Line 7: the loop finished normally. Without try, the program would have stopped at "x7". ### Several except blocks, and the message except SomeError as e: stores the exception in the variable e; printing e shows its message. You can stack several except blocks for different types, and Python uses the first one that matches. ~~~python pumps = {"P1": 30, "P2": 12} for name, hours in [("P1", 5), ("P2", 0), ("P9", 2)]: try: rate = pumps[name] / hours print(name, "pumps", rate, "litres per hour") except ZeroDivisionError as e: print(name, "ran for 0 hours:", e) except KeyError as e: print("Unknown pump:", e) ~~~ - Line 4: looks up the pump, then divides. For P1 the rate is 6.0. - Lines 6 to 7: for P2, dividing by 0 raises ZeroDivisionError; its message is division by zero. - Lines 8 to 9: for P9, pumps["P9"] raises KeyError; printing e shows the missing key, 'P9'. ### Let int() decide int() ignores spaces around the number and accepts a minus sign, but refuses decimals and empty text. So do not try to guess with string tests: call int() and catch the failure. ~~~python for text in [" 4", "-2", "3.5", ""]: try: print(f"[{text}] gives", int(text)) except ValueError: print(f"[{text}] is not a whole number") ~~~ - Prints [ 4] gives 4 and [-2] gives -2, then rejects 3.5 and the empty text. ### A word about RobotError from robot import * also brings in RobotError, the exception Bit raises when it hits a wall, falls in a hole or uses a wrong code. Catching it cannot undo the crash: WARDEN's alarm has already gone off and the run fails. For moves, look first with front() and here(). Keep try for bad data.
goal: Walk to the terminal and scan it: you get a list of texts. Add up every text that int() accepts, and for every text it refuses say Garbled: followed by the text. Then unlock door A with the sum and reach the exit.

title: Lying pump sensors
story: A row of pump terminals lines the drain tunnel. Some are silent, and WARDEN has hacked others to report impossible water levels. A real level is a whole number from 0 to 9. Door A opens with the sum of the honest ones.
power: ### else and finally Two optional blocks complete try. else: runs only if the try block raised nothing. finally: runs every time, error or not, which is perfect for clean-up. ~~~python for text in ["3", "x"]: try: n = int(text) except ValueError: print(text, "is invalid") else: print(text, "doubled is", n * 2) finally: print("checked", text) ~~~ - Lines 4 to 5: run for "x" only. - Lines 6 to 7: run for "3" only, printing 3 doubled is 6. - Lines 8 to 9: run in both rounds. The order is always: try, except, else, finally. Using else keeps the try block short: only the line that can fail goes inside. ### try inside a function A return inside try or except works like anywhere else, so a function can hand back a fallback value when something goes wrong. ~~~python def to_number(text): try: return float(text) except ValueError: return None print(to_number("2.5")) print(to_number("two")) print(to_number("two") is None) ~~~ - Line 3: if float() works, its result is returned at once. - Lines 4 to 5: if it raises, the function returns None instead. - Line 8: is None is the proper way to test for None: prints True. ### raise: your own errors Sometimes a value is fine for Python but wrong for your program, like a water level of 12 on a 0 to 9 gauge. raise ValueError("message") creates an exception and throws it, which stops the function immediately. When a function does not catch an exception, it travels up to whoever called the function, and the caller can catch it there. ~~~python def parse_quantity(text): qty = int(text) if qty < 1: raise ValueError("quantity must be at least 1") return qty for text in ["4", "0", "lots"]: try: print("OK:", parse_quantity(text)) except ValueError as e: print("Rejected", text, "because:", e) ~~~ - Line 2: for "lots", int() already raises. The function has no try, so the exception travels out to the caller by itself. - Lines 3 to 4: for "0", the conversion works but the value is too small, so we raise our own ValueError. Line 5 does not run. - Lines 6 to 10: the caller catches both kinds of failure the same way. ### Common mistakes - A bare except: with no type: it also hides typos and bugs in your own code. Name the exception you expect. - Catching an error and doing nothing, so problems vanish silently. - Putting too much code inside try. Keep only the lines that can fail, and use else for the rest. - Forgetting that raise stops the function: code after it in the same block never runs.
goal: Write read_level(text): it returns int(text), and raises ValueError when the level is below 0 or above 9. Walk to door A. On each terminal, scan a dict like {"pump": "P1", "level": "4"} and say P1 reads 4, or P1 is silent when the "level" key is missing, or P1 is lying when read_level refuses it. Unlock the door with the sum of the honest levels and exit.

title: The flood log
story: Bit finds WARDEN's log disk still spinning in a dry corner. Every event of the night is written there, one line each, and somewhere among them is the line where WARDEN set the code of door A.
power: Programs often need data that lives longer than the program itself: a log, a list, a report. Text files are the simplest way to read data in and save results out. Here files live on a sandbox disk (see the Files tab), and each run starts from a fresh copy. ### Opening and reading a whole file open(name) opens a file and gives you a file object, a handle you read from. The with statement opens it, gives it the name written after as, and closes it automatically when the indented block ends, even if an error happens. f.read() returns the whole content as one string. ~~~python with open("pumps.txt", "w") as f: f.write("pump 1 ok\npump 2 flooded\n") with open("pumps.txt") as f: text = f.read() print(text) print(len(text), "characters") ~~~ - Lines 1 to 2: create a small file to play with (writing is explained in the next mission). - Line 3: opens pumps.txt for reading and names the file object f. - Line 4: reads everything into the string text. - Line 5: we are outside the with block, so the file is closed, but text keeps its value. - Line 6: counts the characters, including the invisible line breaks. Each line of a text file ends with a newline character, written "\n" in Python. It is what makes the text jump to the next line. ### Reading line by line A file object can go in a for loop: each round gives the next line as a string, still ending with "\n". strip() removes it, together with any spaces at both ends. ~~~python with open("pumps.txt", "w") as f: f.write("pump 1 ok\n pump 2 flooded\n") with open("pumps.txt") as f: for line in f: print(len(line), line.strip()) ~~~ - Line 4: line is "pump 1 ok\n" in the first round, then the next line. - Line 5: len(line) counts the newline (10 for the first line), while line.strip() is the clean text, without the leading spaces of the second line. Why strip? print() adds its own line break, so printing the raw line would leave an empty line after each one. ### Finding a line Inside the loop you can test each line like any string. "CODE" in line is true when the text contains CODE, and split() cuts a line into words. ~~~python with open("events.log", "w") as f: f.write("08:00 INFO start\n08:05 CODE vault 3141\n") with open("events.log") as f: for line in f: if "CODE" in line: words = line.strip().split() print(words, words[-1]) ~~~ - Line 7: prints the list of words, then the last one: 3141.
goal: Read logs/warden.log line by line. When a line contains CODE, say that line without its spaces and newline, and keep its last word as the code (as text: some codes start with 0). Then unlock door A and reach the exit.

title: The repair report
story: The damage log is full of holes, like everything else down here. The maintenance door only opens for a unit that files a proper repair report: numbered, clean, and signed. WARDEN counts the lines before it lets anyone through.
power: ### Writing and appending open(name, "w") opens a file for writing. The second argument is the mode: - "r": read (the default, used when you give no mode). - "w": write. It creates the file, or empties it if it already exists. - "a": append, which adds to the end and keeps what is there. f.write(text) writes a string. It does not add a line break, so you add "\n" yourself. ~~~python with open("shopping.txt", "w") as f: f.write("milk\n") f.write("eggs\n") with open("shopping.txt", "a") as f: f.write("bread\n") with open("shopping.txt") as f: print(f.read()) ~~~ - Line 1: creates shopping.txt and opens it for writing. - Lines 2 to 3: write two lines, each with its own \n. - Lines 4 to 5: open the file again in append mode and add a third line at the end. - Lines 6 to 7: read it back: milk, eggs, bread. With "w" on line 4 instead, milk and eggs would be gone. ### enumerate: numbering items as you loop enumerate(collection) gives you pairs of (position, item) in a for loop. Positions start at 0, or at any number you choose with start=. ~~~python colors = ["red", "green", "blue"] for i, color in enumerate(colors): print(i, color) for i, color in enumerate(colors, start=1): print(f"{i}. {color}") ~~~ - Line 3: prints 0 red, 1 green, 2 blue. - Line 5: with start=1: 1. red, 2. green, 3. blue. ### Filter, then save A common job: read lines, keep only the useful ones, write the result to a new file. A blank line strips down to the empty string "", and an empty string counts as false in an if, so if line.strip() keeps only lines with real content. ~~~python with open("draft.txt", "w") as f: f.write("alpha\n\nbeta\n \ngamma\n") with open("draft.txt") as f: words = [line.strip() for line in f if line.strip()] print(words, len(words)) with open("clean.txt", "w") as out: for word in words: out.write(word.upper() + "\n") with open("clean.txt") as f: print(f.read()) ~~~ - Line 4: words becomes ['alpha', 'beta', 'gamma']: the empty line and the line of spaces are gone. - Lines 6 to 8: write each word in capitals, one per line. - Lines 9 to 10: read the result back. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting "\n" in write(), so everything ends up on one line. - Opening with "w" when you meant "a": the old content is wiped. - Forgetting strip(), so blank lines that hold spaces look non-empty. - Writing outside the with block: the file is already closed there.
goal: Read logs/damage.log, keep the non-empty lines (stripped), and store how many there are in line_count. Write them to repair.txt numbered from 1, like 1. pump 2 cracked, then open the file again in append mode and add a last line signed B-17. Door A opens with line_count.

title: Overdue inspection
story: Two pressure doors guard the pump room. Door A opens with the number of days since the last inspection, door B with the day of the month of the next one, due 30 days after the date on the second terminal. Counting days by hand across months is how robots end up in the water.
power: Python comes with a huge standard library: ready-made tools for maths, dates, counting, randomness and much more. Before writing a helper yourself, check whether it already exists. It usually does. ### import: loading a module A module is a file of Python code you can reuse. import name loads it; then you reach what it contains with a dot: module.thing. ~~~python import math print(math.sqrt(16)) print(math.pi) print(math.floor(7.9), math.ceil(7.1)) ~~~ - Line 2: math.sqrt is the square root function: prints 4.0. - Line 3: math.pi is a value, not a function, so no brackets: 3.141592653589793. - Line 4: floor rounds down and ceil rounds up: 7 8. ### from ... import: taking just what you need from module import a, b brings in specific names, so you use them without the module prefix. That is exactly what from robot import * does: the star means "every public name". And abs() needs no import at all: it is a built-in function that gives the distance from zero, so it drops the minus sign. ~~~python from math import sqrt, pi print(sqrt(25), round(pi, 2)) print(abs(-59), abs(59)) ~~~ - Line 2: prints 5.0 3.14. - Line 3: prints 59 59. ### Turning text into dates Dates often arrive as text, like "2026-03-01". The datetime module contains a type also called datetime. Its function strptime(text, format) ("string parse time") reads text according to a format. In the format, %Y means a 4-digit year, %m a 2-digit month and %d a 2-digit day; other characters, like -, must match exactly. ~~~python from datetime import datetime d = datetime.strptime("2026-03-01", "%Y-%m-%d") print(d) print(d.year, d.month, d.day) ~~~ - Line 1: imports the datetime type from the datetime module (same name, two different things). - Line 3: prints 2026-03-01 00:00:00: a date at midnight. - Line 4: its parts are attributes, read with a dot: 2026 3 1. ### Date arithmetic: timedelta and .days Subtracting one datetime from another gives a timedelta: a duration. Its .days attribute is the number of whole days. If the first date is the earlier one, the result is negative, and abs() makes it positive. Adding a timedelta to a date moves forward in time. ~~~python from datetime import datetime, timedelta fmt = "%Y-%m-%d" start = datetime.strptime("2026-02-20", fmt) end = datetime.strptime("2026-03-05", fmt) gap = end - start print(gap, gap.days) print((start - end).days, abs((start - end).days)) later = start + timedelta(days=30) print(later, later.day) ~~~ - Line 6: prints 13 days, 0:00:00 13. Python knows February 2026 has 28 days, leap years included. - Line 7: the other way round gives -13; abs() turns it into 13. - Line 9: 30 days after 20 February is 22 March: prints 2026-03-22 00:00:00 22. ### Common mistakes - Using a module without importing it first: NameError. - Writing math.pi(): pi is a value, not a function. - A wrong format: %M means minutes, not months. Months are %m. - Forgetting .days: subtracting dates gives a timedelta, not a number.
goal: Terminal 1 gives two dates (in any order): say Days since inspection: and the number of days between them, and unlock door A with it. Terminal 2 gives one date: the next inspection is 30 days later. Say Next inspection day: and its day of the month, unlock door B with it, and exit.

title: Counting the debris
story: A jammed keypad keeps typing the same letters over and over into the flood terminal. WARDEN set door A to the letter it presses most. Past the door, a sorting terminal lists the parts the water washed in, and the repair crew will need the two most common ones.
power: ### Counting with Counter Counter, from the collections module, counts how many times each item appears in a string (each character) or a list. It behaves like a dict of counts. most_common(n) returns the n most frequent items as a list of (item, count) tuples, biggest first. ~~~python from collections import Counter counts = Counter("banana") print(counts) print(counts["a"], counts["z"]) top = counts.most_common(1) print(top) print(top[0], top[0][0]) ~~~ - Line 2: counts each letter: b once, a three times, n twice. - Line 3: prints Counter({'a': 3, 'n': 2, 'b': 1}). - Line 4: read a count like a dict: 3. A missing item gives 0 instead of an error. - Line 6: most_common(1) returns a list holding one tuple: [('a', 3)]. - Line 7: top[0] is the tuple ('a', 3), and top[0][0] is the item itself: a. It works on lists too, and the tuples unpack nicely in a for loop: ~~~python from collections import Counter parts = ["bolt", "nut", "bolt", "gear", "bolt", "nut"] for part, count in Counter(parts).most_common(2): print(part, count) ~~~ - Prints bolt 3 then nut 2. ### replace: cleaning text before counting text.replace(old, new) returns a copy of a string with every old replaced by new. Replacing spaces with nothing removes them, so spaces do not win the count. ~~~python from collections import Counter text = "to be or not" print(text.replace(" ", "")) print(Counter(text).most_common(1)) print(Counter(text.replace(" ", "")).most_common(1)) ~~~ - Line 3: prints tobeornot. - Line 4: with spaces, the space is the most common character: [(' ', 3)]. - Line 5: without them: [('o', 3)]. ### random: picking by chance The random module makes random choices. random.choice(list) picks one item; random.randint(1, 6) gives a whole number from 1 to 6, both included. Run this a few times: the result changes, which is why games use it and why checked answers never do. ~~~python import random print(random.choice(["heads", "tails"])) print(random.randint(1, 6)) ~~~ ### Common mistake most_common() returns a list of tuples, so you need two indexes to reach the item: most_common(1)[0][0].
goal: Terminal 1 gives text with spaces: unlock door A with its most common letter, spaces ignored. Terminal 2 gives a list of parts: say the two most common, each as part count, then reach the exit.

title: Bit's first drone
story: Above the basement, the Workshop is still lit. Benches, spare rotors, a fabricator waiting for a blueprint. Bit cannot squeeze into the ventilation shafts, but a drone could. The flight terminal lists which drones to build and how far each one flies.
power: A class lets you create your own type of value, bundling data with the actions that work on it. A drone has a name and a distance flown (data) and it can fly (an action). ### A class and its objects class Name: defines a blueprint. Calling the class like a function, Name(...), builds an object (also called an instance) from it. A function defined inside a class is called a method. The special method __init__ (two underscores on each side, said "dunder init") runs automatically when an object is created. Its first parameter, self, is the new object; writing self.something = value stores an attribute: a variable that belongs to that object. ~~~python class Dog: def __init__(self, name, age): self.name = name self.age = age rex = Dog("Rex", 3) fido = Dog("Fido", 7) print(rex.name, rex.age) print(fido.name, fido.age) rex.age = 4 print(rex.age, fido.age) ~~~ - Line 1: starts the class Dog. Class names start with a capital letter by convention. - Line 2: __init__, with self first, then the values we want. - Lines 3 to 4: store the arguments as attributes of the new object. - Line 5: Dog("Rex", 3) creates an object. Python calls __init__ with self set to that new object. You never pass self yourself. - Line 6: a second, separate object. - Lines 7 to 8: read attributes with a dot: Rex 3 and Fido 7. - Lines 9 to 10: attributes can be changed, and changing rex does not touch fido: 4 7. ### Methods: behaviour that uses the object's data Other methods also take self first, so they can read and change the object's attributes. You call them with a dot, obj.method(arguments), and Python fills in self for you. Not every attribute has to come from a parameter: some start with a fixed value. ~~~python class Counter: def __init__(self): self.value = 0 def increment(self, step=1): self.value += step return self.value def show(self): return f"counter at {self.value}" clicks = Counter() print(clicks.increment()) print(clicks.increment(5)) print(clicks.value, clicks.show()) ~~~ - Lines 2 to 3: every new counter starts at 0; no parameter needed. - Line 4: increment has a parameter step that defaults to 1. - Line 5: += adds to the attribute stored on this particular object. - Line 6: returns the new value to the caller. - Line 10: clicks.increment() runs the method with self = clicks: prints 1. - Line 11: step is 5: prints 6. - Line 12: reads the attribute directly, then calls show: 6 counter at 6. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting self as the first parameter of a method: Python complains about the number of arguments. - Writing distance = 0 instead of self.distance = 0. Without self., it is a local variable that vanishes when the method ends. - Misspelling __init__ (two underscores on each side), so it never runs.
goal: Write a class Drone: Drone(name) stores name and starts distance at 0; fly(squares) adds to the distance and returns the new total; report() returns text like Gnat flew 7. The terminal gives pairs [name, list of flights]: build each drone, fly its flights, say its report. Door A opens with the total distance of all drones.
hint: Inside the loop, drone = Drone(name) builds a fresh drone each round; fly() changes self.distance.

assert t.report() == 'Test flew 5', 'report() should return text like "Test flew 5".'

title: A drone that says no
story: The first drone flew until its battery died in a shaft, and Bit had to fish it out with a magnet. The new model must refuse any trip it cannot finish. WARDEN's flight plan is full of traps: zero-length trips, negative ones, and trips far too long.
power: ### Default values in __init__ __init__ is a normal function, so its parameters can have defaults. And some attributes do not come from parameters at all: they start with a fixed value. ~~~python class Player: def __init__(self, name, score=0): self.name = name self.score = score self.level = 1 ann = Player("Ann") bob = Player("Bob", 50) print(ann.name, ann.score, ann.level) print(bob.name, bob.score, bob.level) ~~~ - Line 2: score is optional and defaults to 0. - Line 5: level is not a parameter: every player starts at level 1. - Lines 8 to 9: print Ann 0 1 and Bob 50 1. ### Protecting an object: check first, then change Methods are the right place to refuse bad requests. Check first, raise a ValueError if something is wrong, and only then change the attribute. Because raise stops the method immediately, a refused request leaves the object untouched. A method may need several checks one after the other, each with its own raise. ~~~python class Thermostat: def __init__(self, target=20): self.target = target def set_target(self, degrees): if degrees < 5: raise ValueError("too cold") if degrees > 30: raise ValueError("too hot") self.target = degrees return self.target t = Thermostat() print(t.set_target(22)) for wish in [80, 2]: try: t.set_target(wish) except ValueError as e: print("Refused:", e) print(t.target) ~~~ - Lines 5 to 8: the checks come first. Any failed check raises and the method stops. - Lines 9 to 10: only reached for valid values: update, then return the new target. - Line 12: 22 is valid: prints 22. - Lines 13 to 17: 80 and 2 are refused; each message is printed. - Line 18: prints 22: the failed calls changed nothing. ### Common mistake Changing the attribute before checking, so a refused request still changes the object. Validate, raise if needed, then change and return.
goal: Write Drone(name, battery=100) with trips starting at 0. fly(distance) raises ValueError("distance must be positive") for 0 or less, ValueError("battery too low") when the distance is more than the battery, and otherwise uses up that much battery, counts the trip and returns the battery left. Scan the plan (battery and trips), build a drone called Scout, try every trip: say Trip 10 done, battery 30 or Refused: and the message. Then say Trips: and the count, and unlock door A with the battery left.
hint: Both checks come before self.battery -= distance; the caller wraps each fly() in try/except ValueError as e.

t = Drone('T')

title: A family of drones
story: A crate of flood pumps blocks the Workshop exit, and one drone cannot lift it. Bit needs a team: Lifters with arms, Floaters that only hover. They share most of their code, so Bit designs one parent class and two children. The fabricator flags any design with more than four arms as overloaded.
power: Inheritance lets one class reuse and adapt another. You write the shared part once, in a parent class, and only the differences in each child. ### A subclass inherits everything Write class Child(Parent): to create a subclass. The child gets all the parent's methods for free, __init__ included. If the child defines a method with the same name, its own version is used instead: this is called overriding. pass means "nothing here", for a class that adds nothing. ~~~python class Animal: def __init__(self, name): self.name = name def speak(self): return "..." def intro(self): return f"I am {self.name}" class Dog(Animal): def speak(self): return "Woof" class Fish(Animal): pass rex = Dog("Rex") nemo = Fish("Nemo") print(rex.intro(), rex.speak()) print(nemo.intro(), nemo.speak()) ~~~ - Line 8: Dog(Animal) means a Dog is a kind of Animal. - Lines 9 to 10: Dog overrides speak. - Line 13: Dog has no __init__, so Python uses Animal's: rex.name is "Rex". - Line 15: intro comes from Animal, speak from Dog: I am Rex Woof. - Line 16: Fish keeps everything from Animal: I am Nemo .... ### Class attributes A variable written directly in the class body (not inside a method, not on self) is a class attribute, shared by every object of that class. Methods read it through self, which looks on the object first, then on its class, then on the parent class. A subclass overrides it by giving it a new value in its own body. ~~~python class Vehicle: wheels = 4 def describe(self): return f"{self.wheels} wheels" class Bike(Vehicle): wheels = 2 print(Vehicle().describe()) print(Bike().describe()) print(Bike.wheels) ~~~ - Line 8: the method comes from Vehicle, but self is a Bike, so self.wheels is 2: 2 wheels. - Line 9: you can read it from the class itself too: 2. ### Formatting numbers with :.2f Inside an f-string, a colon after the value adds a format. :.2f means "a decimal number with exactly 2 digits after the point": it rounds if needed and adds zeros if missing. math.pi is the number pi; a circle's area is pi times the radius squared. ~~~python import math print(f"{math.pi:.2f}") print(f"{10:.2f}") print(f"{math.pi * 3 ** 2:.1f}") ~~~ - Prints 3.14, 10.00, then the area of a circle of radius 3 with 1 decimal: 28.3. ### Parent methods that rely on the child A parent method can call self.something(), and Python runs the version from the object's own class. So the parent writes the general recipe and each child fills in its detail. If a child forgets, the parent's version should complain: raise NotImplementedError is Python's standard way to say "a subclass must provide this". ~~~python class Employee: title = "Employee" def monthly_pay(self): raise NotImplementedError def summary(self): return f"{self.title} earns {self.monthly_pay():.2f}" class Hourly(Employee): title = "Hourly" def __init__(self, rate, hours): self.rate, self.hours = rate, hours def monthly_pay(self): return self.rate * self.hours print(Hourly(15.5, 120).summary()) try: Employee().summary() except NotImplementedError: print("Employee alone has no pay rule") ~~~ - Line 6: summary uses self.title and self.monthly_pay(). - Line 10: sets two attributes at once with tuple unpacking. - Line 13: Employee's summary runs, but self is an Hourly, so its pay rule is used: Hourly earns 1860.00. - Lines 14 to 17: a plain Employee reaches the parent's monthly_pay, which raises. ### super(): extending instead of replacing When a child overrides a method but still wants the parent's version to run, it calls super().method(...). Most often in __init__: the parent sets up its attributes, then the child adds its own. isinstance(obj, Class) checks an object's family, and issubclass(Child, Parent) checks the classes themselves. ~~~python class Animal: def __init__(self, name): self.name = name class Cat(Animal): def __init__(self, name, indoor): super().__init__(name) self.indoor = indoor tom = Cat("Tom", True) print(tom.name, tom.indoor) print(isinstance(tom, Cat), isinstance(tom, Animal)) print(issubclass(Cat, Animal)) ~~~ - Line 6: runs Animal's __init__, which sets self.name. Line 7 then adds Cat's own attribute. - Lines 10 to 11: a Cat is also an Animal: True True, then True. ### Your own exceptions Exceptions are classes too, and they inherit from Exception. A one-line subclass gives you an error type with its own name, which callers can catch separately. RobotError is exactly that: class RobotError(Exception): pass. ~~~python class FloodError(Exception): pass def check_level(cm): if cm > 50: raise FloodError(f"water at {cm} cm") return "dry enough" for cm in [10, 80]: try: print(check_level(cm)) except FloodError as e: print("Flood!", e) print(issubclass(FloodError, Exception)) ~~~ - Lines 1 to 2: a new exception type, with everything inherited from Exception. - Line 5: raised and caught like ValueError: prints Flood! water at 80 cm. ### Common mistakes - Writing class Lifter: without (Drone): no inheritance at all. - Calling a method without self. inside another method: NameError. - Forgetting the brackets: self.lift is the method itself, self.lift() is its result. - Overriding __init__ and forgetting super().__init__(...).

The terminal gives [name, arms] pairs, 0 arms meaning a Floater: say each describe() or Rejected: and the error, then unlock door A with the total lift formatted :.2f.

title: Crates that add up
story: Spare parts sit in crates on two shelves. Bit wants to pour one crate into another with a simple +, ask len() how full it is, and check "fuse" in crate. Python can do all of that for your own class, if you teach it how.
power: Why does + work on numbers and strings but not on your own objects? Python turns operators and some built-in functions into calls to methods with special names, surrounded by double underscores: dunder methods. Define them, and your objects work with +, ==, len(), in and print() like built-in types. ### __repr__ and __str__: how an object is shown By default, printing an object shows something unhelpful like <__main__.Plain object at 0x7f...>. __repr__(self) must return a string, and Python uses it whenever it needs to show the object: in print(), inside lists, and with the built-in repr(). By habit it looks like the code that builds the object. __str__(self) is an optional friendlier version: print() and str() use it when it exists, while lists and repr() keep using __repr__. ~~~python class Plain: def __init__(self, x): self.x = x class Point: def __init__(self, x, y): self.x = x self.y = y def __repr__(self): return f"Point({self.x}, {self.y})" def __str__(self): return f"the point at {self.x}, {self.y}" print(Plain(1)) p = Point(1, 2) print(p) print([p, Point(0, 0)]) print(repr(p) == "Point(1, 2)", str(p)) ~~~ - Line 12: Plain falls back to the default text, with a memory address. - Line 14: print uses __str__: the point at 1, 2. - Line 15: lists use __repr__: [Point(1, 2), Point(0, 0)]. - Line 16: repr(p) calls p.__repr__(); the text must match exactly, spaces included: True. ### __eq__: deciding when two objects are equal Without help, == on your objects is only True when both sides are the very same object. a == b becomes a.__eq__(b), so self is the left side and other the right side. ~~~python class Card: def __init__(self, rank, suit): self.rank = rank self.suit = suit def __eq__(self, other): return (self.rank, self.suit) == (other.rank, other.suit) a = Card(10, "hearts") b = Card(10, "hearts") c = Card(10, "spades") print(a == b, a == c) print(a != c) ~~~ - Line 6: two tuples are equal when all their items are equal, position by position. - Line 10: True False. Without __eq__, a == b would be False. - Line 11: != automatically gives the opposite of __eq__: True. ### __add__: making + work a + b becomes a.__add__(b). Return a new object built from both sides and leave the originals unchanged, just as 2 + 3 does not change the 2. ~~~python class Money: def __init__(self, cents): self.cents = cents def __add__(self, other): return Money(self.cents + other.cents) def __repr__(self): return f"Money({self.cents})" lunch = Money(1250) coffee = Money(300) print(lunch + coffee) print(lunch, coffee) ~~~ - Line 10: lunch.__add__(coffee) builds a new object: Money(1550). - Line 11: the originals did not change: Money(1250) Money(300). ### __len__ and __contains__: len() and in Built-in functions and keywords call dunder methods too: len(x) calls x.__len__(), and item in x calls x.__contains__(item), which returns True or False. ~~~python class Playlist: def __init__(self, songs): self.songs = songs def __len__(self): return len(self.songs) def __contains__(self, song): return song in self.songs mix = Playlist(["a", "b", "c"]) print(len(mix)) print("b" in mix, "z" in mix) ~~~ - Prints 3, then True False. ### Common mistakes - A __repr__ that does not match the expected text exactly. - Using print inside __repr__ instead of return. - Changing self inside __add__ instead of returning a new object.
goal: Write Crate(parts) (a list of part names) with __repr__ giving Crate(['bolt', 'fuse']), __str__ giving crate of 2 parts, __len__, __add__ (a new crate with both lists), __eq__ (same parts list) and __contains__. Scan both terminals into crates, add them, say the result, then say Fuse inside: and True or False. Door A opens with the length of the combined crate.

title: Signal vectors
story: The Workshop's radio mast picks up beacon signals, each one an arrow with an x and a y. WARDEN's door only opens for the doubled sum of all arrows, written like Vec(4, 12). Bit builds a vector class so arrows can be added and scaled with plain + and *.
power: ### __mul__: multiplying by a number a * b becomes a.__mul__(b). The right side does not have to be the same type: here it is a plain number. ~~~python class Money: def __init__(self, cents): self.cents = cents def __mul__(self, factor): return Money(self.cents * factor) def __repr__(self): return f"Money({self.cents})" ticket = Money(900) print(ticket * 3) print(ticket * 0.5) ~~~ - Line 4: factor is whatever stands to the right of *. - Prints Money(2700), then Money(450.0): multiplying by a decimal gives a decimal. Writing the number first, 3 * ticket, would need yet another method; object times number is enough here. ### __abs__ and math.hypot abs(x) calls x.__abs__(). For an arrow on a flat grid, the natural "size" is its length: math.hypot(x, y) gives the straight-line distance from (0, 0) to (x, y), the square root of x squared plus y squared. ~~~python import math print(math.hypot(3, 4)) class Balance: def __init__(self, amount): self.amount = amount def __abs__(self): return abs(self.amount) print(abs(Balance(-40))) ~~~ - Line 2: 9 + 16 = 25, whose square root is 5: prints 5.0. - Line 8: prints 40. ### __lt__: making < and sorted() work a < b becomes a.__lt__(b) ("less than"). Once it exists, sorted(), min() and max() can order your objects. ~~~python class Box: def __init__(self, kg): self.kg = kg def __lt__(self, other): return self.kg < other.kg def __repr__(self): return f"Box({self.kg})" boxes = [Box(7), Box(2), Box(5)] print(Box(1) < Box(3)) print(sorted(boxes), min(boxes)) ~~~ - Line 9: True. - Line 10: [Box(2), Box(5), Box(7)] Box(2). ### Recap of the dunder family - + calls __add__, * calls __mul__, == calls __eq__, < calls __lt__. - abs() calls __abs__, len() calls __len__, in calls __contains__. - Display uses __repr__, and __str__ for print when you give one. - Operators return new objects and leave the originals alone.
goal: Write Vec(x, y) with __repr__ like Vec(1, 2), __add__, __mul__ (by a number), __eq__, __abs__ (its length with math.hypot) and __lt__ (compares lengths). Scan the list of [x, y] signals and turn them into Vecs. Say Weakest: and the shortest one, then Strength: and the length of their sum with 2 decimals. Unlock door A with the sum times 2.

title: The sensor stream
story: Bit reaches the Core, WARDEN's humming heart. Pressure sensors pour out readings faster than any list can hold, so Bit learns to take them in small batches. The last lock pulses to an old rhythm: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, each number the sum of the two before.
power: A generator produces values one at a time, only when asked. It is how Python reads huge files line by line or handles endless streams (sensor readings, new IDs, pages of results) without filling up memory. ### yield: a function that pauses Any function containing the keyword yield becomes a generator function. Calling it does not run its body: it returns a generator object. Each time you ask that object for a value with the built-in next(), the body runs until the next yield, hands out that value, and pauses right there, keeping all its variables. ~~~python def three_steps(): print("starting") yield "one" print("resuming") yield "two" yield "three" g = three_steps() print(type(g).__name__) print(next(g)) print(next(g)) print(next(g)) ~~~ - Line 7: nothing is printed: the body has not started. g is a generator object (line 8 prints generator). - Line 9: next(g) runs from the top: prints starting, reaches yield "one" and pauses; "one" is printed. - Line 10: resumes just after the first yield: prints resuming, then two. - Line 11: resumes again: three. One more next(g) would raise StopIteration: the generator has nothing left. ### Looping over a generator You rarely call next() yourself. A for loop asks for each value and stops cleanly at the end, and list() collects all the values. ~~~python def countdown(n): while n > 0: yield n n -= 1 for x in countdown(3): print("tick", x) print(list(countdown(5))) gen = countdown(2) print(list(gen), list(gen)) ~~~ - Lines 5 to 6: tick 3, tick 2, tick 1. - Line 7: [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]. - Line 9: a generator can be used only once. The first list() empties it, so the second gives []. Call the function again for a fresh one. ### Infinite generators and islice Since values are computed only on demand, a generator may loop forever with while True:. The caller decides how many values to take. islice(generator, n), from the itertools module, takes just the first n. ~~~python from itertools import islice def odd_numbers(): n = 1 while True: yield n n += 2 print(list(islice(odd_numbers(), 5))) for value in odd_numbers(): if value > 7: break print(value) ~~~ - Line 7: [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]. Never call list() on an endless generator without islice: it would never finish. - Lines 8 to 11: a for loop with break works too: 1, 3, 5, 7. ### Updating two variables at once a, b = x, y assigns several variables in one line. Python computes everything on the right first, using the old values, and only then assigns. That makes swaps and "new pair from the old pair" updates easy. ~~~python a, b = 1, 10 a, b = b, a print(a, b) a, b = b, a + b print(a, b) ~~~ - Line 2: the right side is (10, 1), so the values swap: prints 10 1. - Line 4: the right side uses the old values: b is 1 and a + b is 11. Prints 1 11. Writing a = b and b = a + b on two lines would give a different result, because the second line would already see the new a. ### yield inside a for loop yield can sit inside a for loop, handing out one result per round. Two helpers are useful here: range(start, stop, step) jumps by step, and a slice that goes past the end of a list simply stops at the end, with no error. ~~~python letters = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"] print(letters[3:10]) print(list(range(0, 10, 3))) def pairs(items): for i in range(len(items) - 1): yield (items[i], items[i + 1]) print(list(pairs(letters))) ~~~ - Line 2: only two items exist from index 3: ['d', 'e']. - Line 3: from 0, jumping by 3, below 10: [0, 3, 6, 9]. - Line 7: each item with its neighbour: [('a', 'b'), ('b', 'c'), ('c', 'd'), ('d', 'e')]. ### Generator expressions A comprehension written in round brackets instead of square ones is a generator expression: same syntax, but values come one by one instead of being stored in a list. Inside a function call, the extra brackets can be dropped. ~~~python squares = (n * n for n in range(5)) print(type(squares).__name__) print(sum(squares)) print(max(len(w) for w in ["fig", "banana", "kiwi"])) ~~~ - Line 1: nothing is computed yet. - Line 3: sum() pulls 0, 1, 4, 9, 16 one by one: 30. - Line 4: the longest word length: 6. ### Common mistakes - Using return instead of yield: the function hands back one value and ends. - Calling list() on an endless generator. - Reusing a generator that is already used up.

Terminal 2 gives a number n: door B opens with the n-th value of fib() (the last of the first n).

title: Every move on the record
story: Deep in the Core, the corridors twist and the doors keep score. WARDEN's last checkpoint opens only with the exact number of steps Bit took to reach it, and the route comes from a terminal as a string of letters. Bit cannot count by hand, so it wraps its own motors in a counter.
power: A decorator adds extra behaviour to a function without touching the function's own code: logging every call, counting it, timing it, checking permissions. You switch it on with one line, @name, just above a def. ### Functions are values In Python a function is an object, like a number or a string. Its name without brackets refers to the function itself. You can store it in another variable, put it in a dict, pass it to another function, and read its attributes, such as __name__, its name as text. ~~~python def shout(text): return text.upper() + "!" yell = shout print(yell("hello")) print(shout.__name__, yell.__name__) def apply_twice(func, value): return func(func(value)) print(apply_twice(shout, "hi")) actions = {"s": shout, "l": str.lower} print(actions["s"]("go"), actions["l"]("GO")) ~~~ - Line 3: no brackets, so nothing runs: yell now refers to the same function. - Line 5: both names lead to one function, which keeps its original name: shout shout. - Lines 6 to 8: func is a parameter holding a function: prints HI!! - Lines 9 to 10: a dict of functions, looked up by a letter and then called: GO! go. ### Functions inside functions A def can sit inside another function. The inner function can use the outer function's variables, and the outer function can return the inner function, which keeps remembering those variables. ~~~python def make_multiplier(n): def multiply(x): return x * n return multiply double = make_multiplier(2) triple = make_multiplier(3) print(double(5), triple(5)) print(double.__name__) ~~~ - Line 4: returns the inner function itself, not a result (no brackets). - Lines 5 to 6: two multiply functions, one remembering 2, one remembering 3. - Line 7: 10 15. Line 8: multiply. ### Passing arguments along with * and ** In a def, *args and **kwargs collect arguments. In a call, the stars do the reverse: *a_tuple spreads its items as positional arguments and **a_dict spreads its pairs as keyword arguments. Together, a function can accept anything and pass it on unchanged. ~~~python def describe(name, age, city="?"): return f"{name}, {age}, from {city}" values = ("Ada", 36) options = {"city": "London"} print(describe(*values, **options)) def pass_along(*args, **kwargs): print("args:", args, "kwargs:", kwargs) return describe(*args, **kwargs) print(pass_along("Bo", age=22)) ~~~ - Line 5: the same as describe("Ada", 36, city="London"). - Lines 7 to 8: prints args: ('Bo',) kwargs: {'age': 22}, then spreads them back out exactly as received. ### Writing a decorator A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a new one, usually an inner wrapper that does something extra and calls the original. Writing @decorator on the line above a def is shorthand for name = decorator(name) right after it. You can also write that line yourself, to wrap a function you did not define, like move. ~~~python def announce(func): def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): print("Calling", func.__name__, "with", args) result = func(*args, **kwargs) print("Got", result) return result return wrapper @announce def add(a, b): return a + b total = add(2, 3) print(total, add.__name__) ~~~ - Line 2: wrapper accepts any arguments, so it fits any function. - Line 4: calls the original with the same arguments and keeps its result. - Line 6: returns that result. Without it, the decorated function would return None. - Lines 8 to 10: @announce means add = announce(add). From now on, add is the wrapper. - Line 11: prints Calling add with (2, 3), then Got 5. - Line 12: prints 5 wrapper: the original name is lost. ### functools.wraps: keeping the original name Tools and tests rely on __name__. Put @functools.wraps(func) above the wrapper's def: it copies the original's name (and description) onto the wrapper. It is itself a decorator, one that takes an argument. ~~~python import functools def announce(func): @functools.wraps(func) def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): print("Calling", func.__name__) return func(*args, **kwargs) return wrapper @announce def greet(name): return f"Hi {name}" print(greet("Ada")) print(greet.__name__) ~~~ - Line 11: prints Calling greet, then Hi Ada. Line 12: greet. ### Decorators that take arguments wraps(func) shows the trick: a function that receives the settings and returns the real decorator. That is one more level of inner function. ~~~python import functools def repeat(times): def decorator(func): @functools.wraps(func) def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): for _ in range(times): result = func(*args, **kwargs) return result return wrapper return decorator @repeat(3) def beep(): print("beep") beep() ~~~ - Line 11: repeat(3) runs first and returns decorator, which then wraps beep. Prints beep three times. ### Attributes on functions Since functions are objects, you can attach your own attributes to them: func.something = value. A decorator can attach one to the wrapper once, then update it on every call, which keeps information between calls. Inside the wrapper, refer to it as wrapper.something. ~~~python import functools def remember_args(func): @functools.wraps(func) def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): wrapper.history.append(args) return func(*args, **kwargs) wrapper.history = [] return wrapper @remember_args def square(n): return n * n print(square.history) print(square(3), square(4)) print(square.history) ~~~ - Line 7: runs only once, when the decorator is applied. It sits after the wrapper's def and outside its body, so it is not reset on each call. - Lines 12 to 14: [], then 9 16, then [(3,), (4,)]. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting return wrapper: the decorated name becomes None. - Forgetting to return the original function's result from the wrapper. - Setting up a counter inside the wrapper body, so it starts over on every call. - Forgetting @functools.wraps(func), so __name__ says wrapper.

Move onto the terminal, then follow the route it gives (F forward, L left, R right). Say each function's name and its number of calls, like move 7, then unlock door A with the number of moves and reach the exit.

title: WARDEN's mail
story: WARDEN talks to the night crew by message, and its terminals still hold the last ones: long, noisy, full of numbers. Somewhere in each message is a four-digit door code, and a list of addresses Bit will need later to warn the crew. Reading them by eye is slow; patterns are fast.
power: A regular expression (regex) is a tiny pattern language for finding text by its shape: "some digits", "a word, an @, a domain", "two digits, a dash, two digits". It is how you pull emails, phone numbers, dates or codes out of messy text. ### re.findall and raw strings Python's regex tools live in the module re. re.findall(pattern, text) returns a list of every piece of text that matches. In a pattern, \d means any digit from 0 to 9, and + after something means "one or more of it, as many as possible". Write patterns as raw strings, r"...": the r tells Python to leave backslashes alone, so \d reaches the regex engine untouched. ~~~python import re text = "Order 66 shipped 3 boxes on day 120" print(re.findall(r"\d", text)) print(re.findall(r"\d+", text)) print(re.findall(r"\d+", "no numbers here")) ~~~ - Line 3: \d alone matches single digits: ['6', '6', '3', '1', '2', '0']. - Line 4: \d+ grabs whole runs of digits: ['66', '3', '120']. Results are always strings. - Line 5: nothing matches, so the list is empty: []. ### More building blocks - \w: a word character (letter, digit or underscore). \s: whitespace (space, tab, newline). - \D, \W, \S: the capital letter means the opposite, for example \D is anything that is not a digit. - .: any single character. To match a real dot, escape it: \. - *: zero or more. {3}: exactly 3 times. Like +, they apply to the thing just before them. ~~~python import re s = "Ada_99 met Bo at 10.30, then Cy at 9.05" print(re.findall(r"\w+", s)) print(re.findall(r"\d+\.\d{2}", s)) print(re.findall(r"\d\d", "2026")) print(re.findall(r"a.", "banana bar")) print(re.findall(r"\S+", "two words"), re.findall(r"\s", "a b\tc")) print(re.findall(r"bo*m", "bm bom boooom")) ~~~ - Line 3: the dot and the comma are not word characters, so 10.30 splits into '10' and '30'. - Line 4: digits, a real dot, then exactly two digits: ['10.30', '9.05']. - Line 5: two digits at a time: ['20', '26']. - Line 6: an a followed by any character, even a space: ['an', 'an', 'a ', 'ar']. - Line 7: runs of non-space: ['two', 'words']; then each whitespace character: [' ', '\t']. - Line 8: o* allows no o at all: ['bm', 'bom', 'boooom']. ### Character sets with [ ] Square brackets match one character from a set: [aeiou] is a vowel, [0-9] a digit range, [\w.] a word character or a dot (inside brackets a dot is literal). A hyphen between two characters means a range, so to include a real hyphen, put it first: [-\w.]. Add + after the set for one or more. ~~~python import re mails = "Mail ana@shop.fr or ana.b@shop.fr" print(re.findall(r"[aeiou]", "regular")) print(re.findall(r"\w+@\w+\.\w+", mails)) print(re.findall(r"[\w.]+@\w+\.\w+", mails)) print(re.findall(r"[-\w]+", "a well-known e-mail")) ~~~ - Line 3: each vowel separately: ['e', 'u', 'a']. - Line 4: \w+ cannot cross the dot in ana.b, so the second match is cut: ['ana@shop.fr', 'b@shop.fr']. - Line 5: [\w.]+ accepts dots in the name part: both addresses come out whole. - Line 6: hyphen first in the set, so hyphenated words stay whole: ['a', 'well-known', 'e-mail']. Real addresses can also contain hyphens, in the name and in the domain: add them to the sets where they may appear. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting the r before the pattern string. - A bare . where you meant a real dot: write \.. - A hyphen in the middle of a set, which makes a range: put it first.
goal: Scan the message. Say every email address in it, in order (names and domains may contain dots and hyphens). The door code is the only run of exactly four digits: unlock door A with it and reach the exit.

title: The override pin
story: WARDEN keeps an emergency override in its own logs, in case it ever locks itself out. The pin is there, but broken up with dashes and spaces so no human could copy it at a glance. Bit also wants the exact times WARDEN was seen writing, for the final report.
power: ### Groups: ( ) and (?: ) Round brackets group pieces, so a quantifier applies to the whole group: (ab)+ means "ab, repeated". But careful: with a normal group, findall returns only what the group matched, not the whole match. Write (?: ... ), a non-capturing group, to group without changing what findall returns. ~~~python import re log = "Start 08:58:12, error 09:02:45, end 10.05.11" print(re.findall(r"\d{2}(:\d{2}){2}", log)) print(re.findall(r"\d{2}(?::\d{2}){2}", log)) print(re.findall(r"\d{2}(?:[.:]\d{2}){2}", log)) ~~~ - Line 3: two digits, then the group "colon and two digits" twice. With a normal group, findall returns only the group's last match: [':12', ':45']. Not what we want. - Line 4: (?: makes a plain group, so whole matches come back: ['08:58:12', '09:02:45']. - Line 5: the separator is now a set, [.:], a dot or a colon, so the third time matches too. ### re.search and .group re.search(pattern, text) finds only the first match. It returns a match object, or None if nothing matches. On a match, .group(0) is the whole match, and .group(1), .group(2) are the captured groups, counted from the left. ~~~python import re m = re.search(r"(\w+)@([\w.]+)", "contact: bo@acme.com today") print(m.group(0)) print(m.group(1), m.group(2)) print(re.search(r"\d", "no digits")) ~~~ - Line 2: two capturing groups: the name and the domain. - Line 3: prints bo@acme.com. - Line 4: prints bo acme.com. - Line 5: no match: prints None. Check for None before calling .group when a match might be missing. ### re.sub: replacing matches re.sub(pattern, replacement, text) returns a copy of the text with every match replaced. Replacing with "" deletes the matches. Inside a list comprehension, it cleans a whole list. ~~~python import re print(re.sub(r"\s+", " ", "too many spaces")) print(re.sub(r"\D", "", "+33 (0)6-12")) codes = ["AB-12-CD", "EF 34 GH"] print([re.sub(r"[- ]", "", c) for c in codes]) ~~~ - Line 2: each run of whitespace becomes one space: too many spaces. - Line 3: every non-digit is deleted: 330612. - Line 5: hyphens and spaces removed: ['AB12CD', 'EF34GH']. ### Common mistakes - Using a normal group with findall and getting only pieces back: use (?: ). - Calling .group() on None when search found nothing. ### Recap - re.findall lists all matches, re.search finds the first, re.sub replaces. - \d \w \s and their opposites \D \W \S; . any character; + * {n} repeat. - [...] is one character from a set; ( ) captures, (?: ) groups without capturing.
goal: Scan the log. Say Seen at and each time written as two digits, colon, two digits, colon, two digits (not the ones with dots). Then find door, its letter, pin and the pin made of digits, dashes and spaces with re.search and two groups: say Door, the letter and the pin with only its digits kept. Unlock door A with those digits and exit.
solution:
from robot import *
import re

while here() != "terminal":
    move()
text = scan()
for stamp in re.findall(r"\d{2}(?::\d{2}){2}", text):
    say("Seen at", stamp)
m = re.search(r"door (\w) pin ([-\d ]+)", text)
pin = re.sub(r"\D", "", m.group(2))
say("Door", m.group(1), pin)
while front() != "door":
    move()
unlock(pin)
while not at_exit():
    move()

title: Boss: WARDEN's inventory
story: The final lock is WARDEN's own storeroom. Its stock list sits on disk, deliveries keep arriving at one terminal while WARDEN's drones try to take parts at the other, and the vault door opens only for the exact value of what is left. Bit builds a real inventory manager, everything it learned in one program, and saves the books for the crew.
power: This boss combines classes, dictionaries, exceptions, generator expressions and files in one program: an inventory manager that loads itself from disk and saves itself back. Here are the last few tools. ### Dictionaries inside a dictionary A dict value can itself be a dict: a natural way to store records by name. The outer key is the item name, the inner dict holds its details. Chain the square brackets to reach inside. not in is the opposite of in. And or checks its left side first and stops as soon as something is true, so a test on a missing key can be guarded safely. ~~~python stock = {"pen": {"qty": 10, "price": 1.5}} stock["pen"]["qty"] += 5 stock["ink"] = {"qty": 2, "price": 9.99} print(stock) print(stock["ink"]["price"]) print("pad" in stock, "pad" not in stock) for name in ["pen", "pad"]: print(name, name not in stock or stock[name]["qty"] < 5) ~~~ - Line 2: stock["pen"] is the inner dict, and ["qty"] reaches inside it: 10 + 5 = 15. - Line 3: adds a new record under the key "ink". - Line 6: in checks the outer keys: False True. - Lines 7 to 8: for "pen" the left side is false, so Python checks the quantity: False. For "pad" the left side is already true, so Python never runs stock["pad"], which would raise a KeyError: True. ### setdefault: get it, or create it first d.setdefault(key, default) returns d[key] if the key exists. If not, it first stores default under that key, then returns it. It returns the stored dict itself, not a copy, so changing what it returns changes the record inside d. ~~~python stock = {"pen": {"qty": 10, "price": 1.5}} item = stock.setdefault("pen", {"qty": 0, "price": 2.0}) print(item) item = stock.setdefault("pad", {"qty": 0, "price": 4.0}) item["qty"] += 3 print(stock) ~~~ - Line 2: "pen" exists, so the existing record is returned and the default is ignored. - Line 4: "pad" is missing, so the default record is stored, then returned. - Line 5: changes the stored record through item: pad now has 3. An if name not in stock: check followed by a normal assignment does the same job, if you prefer. ### Looping over values and items .values() gives the inner dicts; .items() gives (key, value) pairs. Generator expressions inside sum() and sorted() build totals and filtered, sorted lists in one line. round(x, 2) keeps 2 decimals, handy for money. ~~~python stock = {"pen": {"qty": 10, "price": 1.5}, "pad": {"qty": 3, "price": 4.0}, "ink": {"qty": 1, "price": 9.99}} for name, info in stock.items(): print(name, info["qty"] * info["price"]) units = sum(info["qty"] for info in stock.values()) print(units) rare = sorted(name for name, info in stock.items() if info["qty"] < 4) print(rare) print(round(10 / 3, 2)) ~~~ - Line 5: 10 + 3 + 1: prints 14. - Line 7: the names whose quantity is below 4, sorted: ['ink', 'pad']. - Line 8: 3.33. ### Saving and loading with json JSON is a text format for data that almost every language can read. json.dump(data, file) writes dicts, lists, strings, numbers and True/False into an open file; indent=2 makes it readable. json.load(file) reads it back as Python dicts and lists. ~~~python import json data = {"pen": {"qty": 10, "price": 1.5}, "tags": ["office", "cheap"]} with open("data.json", "w") as f: json.dump(data, f, indent=2) with open("data.json") as f: print(f.read()) with open("data.json") as f: loaded = json.load(f) print(loaded["pen"]["qty"], loaded == data) ~~~ - Lines 3 to 4: open a file for writing and dump the dict into it. - Lines 5 to 6: show the raw text: it looks almost like Python. - Lines 7 to 9: turn the text back into a dict: 10 True, the round trip kept everything. ### @classmethod: building an object from a file A normal method receives an object as self. A method marked with the decorator @classmethod receives the class itself, by convention named cls, and is called on the class: Settings.from_file(...). Inside it, cls() creates a new object of that class. This is the standard way to write other ways of building an object, like loading one from a file. ~~~python import json with open("config.json", "w") as f: json.dump({"app": "pumps", "debug": True}, f) class Settings: def __init__(self): self.values = {} def get(self, key): return self.values.get(key) @classmethod def from_file(cls, path): s = cls() with open(path) as f: s.values = json.load(f) return s cfg = Settings.from_file("config.json") print(type(cfg).__name__) print(cfg.get("app"), cfg.get("debug")) ~~~ - Line 9: @classmethod changes what the first parameter receives: cls is the class Settings itself. - Line 11: cls() runs __init__ and gives a fresh, empty object, filled on lines 12 to 13. - Line 14: return the finished object. Forgetting this returns None. - Line 15: called on the class, not on an object. - Line 16: type(cfg) is its class, and __name__ its name: Settings. - Line 17: pumps True. ### Common mistakes - Changing a quantity before checking it is allowed: check, raise, then change. - Reading d[name] before checking that name exists: put the not in test first. - Forgetting return at the end of a classmethod that builds an object. - Opening the file with "w" to load it: that empties it.
